items.prose: A designated market maker quotes £3.49 bid and £3.51 ask for 2,000 shares on each side. A buyer and then a seller each trade the full size.
items.question: How much cash does the round trip make, in pounds?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the gain per share on the round trip, then multiply.

byKey.one-side: That is one trade's 1p a share against the mid. The round trip keeps the full 2p.
byKey.per-share: That is one share. Each side traded 2,000.

explain.text: Sell at £3.51, buy at £3.49: 2p a share kept, £40.00 on 2,000 shares.

items.prose: $V = 1{,}200$p, half-spread $s = 3$p, skew $\gamma = 0.5$p per lot. You are short 4 lots, $q = -4$.
items.question: What is your bid, in pence?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find $m = V - \gamma q$ with $q = -4$, then take off $s$.

byKey.wrong-way: You moved the centre down. Short inventory raises it.
byKey.no-skew: You left out the skew of 2p.
byKey.gamma1: You moved the centre 4p, one per lot. Each lot moves it $\gamma = 0.5$p.

explain.text: Short 4 lots, the centre rises $0.5 \times 4 = 2$p to 1,202p. Bid 1,199p and ask 1,205p, so sellers are drawn in.

items.prose: A junior maker loses money to informed traders. She plans to stop quoting whenever she suspects one is around, and to quote only when the flow looks calm.
items.question: Why does this not remove adverse selection?

options.text: Informed traders cannot be told apart from the rest; they simply trade whenever she does quote
It does remove it, so her spread can fall to zero
options.why: You assumed she can spot informed traders. If she could, adverse selection would not exist.

options.text: Because the spread is pure profit anyway
options.why: The spread is the fee that covers losses to the informed, not pure profit.

options.text: Because informed traders only trade in auctions
options.why: Informed traders use every venue, and they prefer the ones where makers quote.

feedback.correct: She cannot see who is informed, so waiting filters nothing.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask whether she can tell an informed order from a noise order before it trades.

explain.text: An informed order looks like any other until the price moves. While she quotes, the share $\alpha$ of informed flow is the same; while she waits, she earns nothing. Only a spread of at least $\alpha\delta$ covers it.

items.prose: An opening auction. The table counts buyers and sellers at each price.
items.question: What is the opening price, in pence?

feedback.correct: At 102p, 900 shares match, the most at any price.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take the smaller side on each row, then the largest of those.

explain.text: The matched amounts are 400, 700, 900, 500 and 200 from 100p up. The most is 900 at 102p, so the share opens at 102p.

items.prose: In a share where arrivals on each side follow $\lambda(s) = 6e^{-s/3}$ a minute, with $s$ in pence.
items.question: Which half-spread maximises expected profit per minute, in pence?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The peak of $2s\lambda_0 e^{-ks}$ is at $s^* = 1/k$.

byKey.k: That is $k$ itself. The peak is at $1/k$.
byKey.lam: $\lambda_0$ sets the height of the curve, not where it peaks.

explain.text: Profit $2s\lambda_0 e^{-ks}$ has slope $2\lambda_0 e^{-ks}(1 - ks)$, zero at $s = 1/k = 3$p. The rate $\lambda_0 = 6$ only scales the profit.

items.prose: Fair value 500p; the value will be 510p or 490p, equally likely; one trader in five is informed. Two buys arrive in a row, from independent traders.
items.question: What is $E[V \mid \text{two buys}]$, in pence, to two decimal places?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each buy multiplies the odds of 510p by $0.6/0.4$.

byKey.one-buy: That is the update after one buy. The second buy is more evidence.
byKey.added: You added 2p per buy. The second buy updates from 0.6, not from 0.5, so the step is smaller.
byKey.prior: You ignored both trades. Each buy is evidence of the high value.

explain.text: Each buy has likelihood 0.6 under 510p and 0.4 under 490p. After two, $P(510) = \tfrac{0.36}{0.36 + 0.16} = \tfrac{9}{13}$. So $E[V] = 490 + 20 \times \tfrac{9}{13} \approx 503.85$p.

items.prose: Lit best bid £8.20, best ask £8.26. You buy 5,000 shares in a dark pool at the lit mid.
items.question: How much do you save against buying at the lit ask, in pounds?

feedback.correct: 3p a share, the half-spread, on 5,000 shares.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The mid is half the spread below the ask.

byKey.full: You saved the whole 6p spread. At mid you save only half of it.
byKey.per-share: That is one share. You bought 5,000.

explain.text: Mid £8.23 is 3p below the ask: £150.00 on 5,000 shares. Only if the dark order fills, though.

items.prose: A maker sets its skew per lot by $\gamma = A\sigma^2\tau$. Volatility doubles, but it now plans to hold positions for half as long.
items.question: By what factor does $\gamma$ change?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Square the change in $\sigma$, then multiply by the change in $\tau$.

byKey.one: You let doubling and halving cancel. $\sigma$ enters squared, so its effect is 4, not 2.
byKey.four: You left out the halving of $\tau$.

explain.text: $\sigma^2$ goes up by 4 and $\tau$ down by 2, so $\gamma$ doubles.

items.prose: A maker quotes a 2p half-spread. In this share 30% of traders are informed about a move of $\pm 10$p.
items.question: What is its expected profit per trade, in pence a share?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Subtract the expected loss to the informed, $\alpha\delta$, from $s$.

byKey.spread: You treated the spread as pure profit. Informed traders cost $0.3 \times 10 = 3$p a trade.
byKey.sign: The size is right but the maker is losing: $2 - 3$ is negative.
byKey.full: One trade earns at most the half-spread.

explain.text: Each trade earns $s = 2$p but costs $\alpha\delta = 3$p on average to the informed. The maker loses 1p a trade and must widen to at least 3p.
